lessons.title: Tajweed: what it is and why it matters
lessons.lede: Tajweed is giving every letter its right and its due when reciting the Quran; it keeps the recitation free of mistakes.

formula.caption: Its point of articulation and the characteristics it always has
Rules that come to it, such as ikhfa' and madd
Reciting as the Quran was revealed

idea.lead: In Arabic, tajweed means making something better. As a term, it means giving every letter its right and its due. A letter's right is its point of articulation and the characteristics that never leave it, such as being whispered or voiced. Its due is what comes to it because of where it stands, such as izhar, ikhfa', madd and tafkhim.
idea.kidsLead: Tajweed means reading the Quran well: saying every letter from its right place, the right way, as the Prophet ﷺ read it.

how.text: The words and letters of the Quran.
Learning its rules is a communal duty (fard kifayah); reciting with tajweed is required of everyone who reads the Quran, as far as they are able.
It keeps the tongue from mistakes in the words of Allah.
It is learned from a skilled teacher, by listening to them and reciting before them, not from books alone.
The lessons in this app follow the riwayah of Hafs from 'Asim, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah: the same reading as the app's Mushaf.

idea.note: Ibn al-Jazari says in his Muqaddimah: «وَالأَخْذُ بِالتَّجْوِيدِ حَتْمٌ لازِمُ ... مَنْ لَمْ يُجَوِّدِ القُرآنَ آثِمُ»: applying tajweed is a firm duty, and whoever does not recite the Quran with tajweed is sinful. Lesson 3 explains clear and hidden mistakes.

quiz.q: What does tajweed mean in Arabic?
quiz.why: Jawwadtu ash-shay' means "I made it better", so tajweed means making better.

quiz.q: What is tajweed, as a term?
options: Reciting the Quran in a beautiful voice
Giving every letter its right and its due
Knowing the meaning of the ayahs
quiz.why: Tajweed is giving every letter its right and its due. A beautiful voice adorns the recitation, but it is not tajweed.

quiz.q: What is a letter's right?
options: Its point of articulation and the characteristics it always has
The rules that come to it
How it is written in the Mushaf
quiz.why: A letter's right is what never leaves it: its point of articulation and its permanent characteristics, such as being whispered or voiced.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of a letter's due?
quiz.why: Ikhfa' comes to noon sakinah because of the letter after it, so it is part of the letter's due. Its point of articulation and being voiced or whispered are its permanent right.

quiz.q: Is reciting with tajweed required of whoever reads the Quran?
quiz.why: Reciting with tajweed is required of everyone who reads the Quran, as far as they are able. Ibn al-Jazari says: «والأخذ بالتجويد حتم لازم» (applying tajweed is a firm duty).

quiz.q: What is the ruling on learning the rules and terms of tajweed?
quiz.why: Learning the rules is a communal duty: when some Muslims do it, the rest are free of blame. Reciting correctly, though, is needed by every reader.

quiz.q: How is tajweed learned properly?
options: By reciting before a skilled teacher
quiz.why: Tajweed is learned by listening and reciting: you hear the teacher, then recite before them and they correct you. Books and apps help, but do not replace that.

lessons.title: The virtue and etiquette of recitation
lessons.lede: Reciting the Quran brings a great reward, and its etiquette joins a present heart with careful reading.

formula.caption: «The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it» (al-Bukhari)

idea.lead: Reciting the Quran is one of the best acts of worship: every letter you read earns a good deed, and each good deed is worth ten. Whoever reads it with difficulty, stumbling over it, has a double reward. Reciting has etiquette that helps the reader be humble and reflect.
idea.kidsLead: Every letter you read from the Quran earns you a good deed, and each good deed is worth ten! We read the Quran with good manners: we make wudu, seek refuge with Allah, read calmly, and think about what it means.

how.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever reads a letter from the Book of Allah has a good deed for it, and a good deed is worth ten like it. I do not say that Alif-Laam-Meem is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, laam is a letter and meem is a letter» (at-Tirmidhi).

The Prophet ﷺ said: «The one who is skilled in the Quran is with the noble, righteous scribes (the angels), and the one who reads the Quran and stumbles over it, finding it hard, has two rewards» (Muslim).
The Prophet ﷺ said: «Read the Quran, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions» (Muslim).
It is recommended to recite in a state of purity, in a clean place, facing the qiblah when possible.

Begin by seeking refuge with Allah. Allah says: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ» (An-Nahl 98): when you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Lesson 4 covers it in detail.
Recite slowly and with tajweed. Allah says: «وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا» (Al-Muzzammil 4): recite the Quran in measured recitation. Do not rush so much that letters are lost.

Think about the meaning of what you read, with a present heart. Allah says: «كِتَابٌ أَنزَلْنَاهُ إِلَيْكَ مُبَارَكٌ لِّيَدَّبَّرُوا آيَاتِهِ» (Sad 29): a blessed Book We revealed to you, so that they may reflect on its ayahs.

idea.note: Reciting the Quran from memory without wudu is allowed; touching the Mushaf requires wudu according to most scholars.

quiz.q: How many good deeds does reading one letter of the Book of Allah earn?
quiz.why: The Prophet ﷺ said: «he has a good deed for it, and a good deed is worth ten like it».

quiz.q: The Prophet ﷺ said: «I do not say that Alif-Laam-Meem is one letter». How many letters is «الم»?
quiz.why: He ﷺ said: «alif is a letter, laam is a letter and meem is a letter», so reading it earns thirty good deeds.

quiz.q: What is the reward of someone who stumbles over the Quran, finding it hard?
quiz.why: Two rewards: one for reciting and one for the effort. So do not give up because it is hard: keep trying and keep learning.

quiz.q: Who are "the best of you" in al-Bukhari's hadith?
options: Those who learn the Quran and teach it
quiz.why: The Prophet ﷺ said: «The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it».

quiz.q: How does the reader begin reciting?
quiz.why: Allah says: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ»: when you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.

quiz.q: What does reflection (tadabbur) mean?
options: Thinking about the meaning of the ayahs
quiz.why: Reflection is thinking about the meaning of what you read; the Quran was revealed «so that they may reflect on its ayahs».

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the etiquette of recitation?
options: Rushing so that letters are lost
quiz.why: Allah commands tarteel, and rushing so that letters are lost goes against it.

lessons.title: Clear and hidden mistakes (lahn)
lessons.lede: Lahn is a mistake in recitation. It is of two kinds: clear, which most people notice, and hidden, which only skilled reciters notice.

formula.caption: An obvious mistake in a letter or a vowel
A mistake in the finer points of reading

idea.lead: In Arabic, lahn means turning away from what is right; as a term, it is a mistake in reciting the Quran. It is of two kinds. Clear lahn is an obvious mistake in a letter or a vowel, whether or not it changes the meaning, and most people notice it. Hidden lahn spoils the finer points of pronunciation without changing a letter or its vowel, and only skilled reciters notice it.
idea.kidsLead: Lahn is a mistake in reading. Some mistakes are big and easy to hear, like saying one letter or vowel instead of another. Some are small and hidden, like leaving out the ghunnah or cutting a madd short. We learn tajweed to avoid both.

how.text: Saying one letter instead of another, such as «الهمد» with haa instead of «الحمد»; one vowel instead of another, such as «أَنْعَمْتُ» instead of «أَنْعَمْتَ», which changes the meaning; or adding or dropping a letter.
Forbidden, by agreement of the scholars, for whoever does it on purpose or neglects learning how to avoid it.
Breaking the tajweed rules while the letter and its vowel stay the same: leaving out the ghunnah, getting a madd's length wrong, or making a light letter heavy.
Less serious than clear lahn. Scholars differ on it: some say it is forbidden, others that it is disliked.

idea.note: Some hidden lahn only experts notice, such as rolling the raa too much or overdoing the ghunnah. The last lesson of the course covers common mistakes in pronouncing the letters in detail.

quiz.q: What does lahn mean in Arabic?
options: Turning away from what is right
quiz.why: In Arabic, lahn means turning away from what is right; in recitation, it is a mistake.

quiz.q: Someone read «الحمد» with haa (ه): «الهمد». What kind of mistake is this?
quiz.why: Saying one letter instead of another is clear lahn, which most people notice.

quiz.q: What kind of mistake is leaving out the ghunnah in ikhfa'?
quiz.why: The letter and its vowel stay the same, but the finer point of reading is lost: this is hidden lahn.

quiz.q: What kind of mistake is reading «أَنْعَمْتَ» with a dammah on the taa?
quiz.why: The vowel changed, and so did the meaning: the favour would belong to the reader. This is clear lahn.

quiz.q: Who notices hidden lahn?
quiz.why: Only those who have learned tajweed well, from a teacher, notice hidden lahn. That is why a reader needs a teacher.

quiz.q: What is the ruling on clear lahn done on purpose?
quiz.why: Clear lahn is forbidden, by agreement of the scholars, for whoever does it on purpose or neglects learning.

quiz.q: Does clear lahn have to change the meaning?
options: No: it may or may not change the meaning
quiz.why: Clear lahn is a mistake in a letter or a vowel, whether or not it changes the meaning.

lessons.title: Isti'adhah and basmalah
lessons.lede: The reader begins with the isti'adhah (seeking refuge with Allah), then the basmalah at the start of every surah except At-Tawbah.

idea.lead: The isti'adhah is saying «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم» (I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan) before reciting, following Allah's words: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ» (An-Nahl 98). The basmalah is saying «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful); it is read at the start of every surah except At-Tawbah. There are several ways to join or separate them and the start of the surah, given below.
idea.kidsLead: Before we read, we say: «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم». At the start of every surah we say: «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم», except Surah At-Tawbah, which we start without it.

how.text: Its best-known wording is «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم». Say it aloud when reciting aloud with someone listening; say it quietly in prayer and when reciting quietly.
It is read at the start of every surah except At-Tawbah. When starting in the middle of a surah, the reader may read it or leave it.
At the start of a surah, four ways are allowed: stop after each; stop after the isti'adhah and join the basmalah to the surah; join the isti'adhah to the basmalah and stop; or join all three.

Three ways are allowed: stop after each; stop at the end of the surah and join the basmalah to the next; or join all three. Joining the end of a surah to the basmalah and then stopping is not allowed, so that the basmalah is not taken as part of the surah before it.
It is read without the basmalah. Between Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah there are three ways: stop, pause briefly (saktah), or join, all without the basmalah.

idea.note: Most scholars say the isti'adhah is recommended; some say it is required. Hafs from 'Asim reads the basmalah between every two surahs, except Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah.

quiz.q: What is the best-known wording of the isti'adhah?
quiz.why: Allah says: «فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ», so its best-known wording is «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم».

quiz.q: Which surah does not begin with the basmalah?
quiz.why: Surah At-Tawbah alone is read without the basmalah at its start.

quiz.q: At the start of a surah, how many ways are there to join or separate the isti'adhah, the basmalah and the surah?
quiz.why: Four: stop after each; stop after the first and join the second to the third; join the first to the second and stop; or join all three.

quiz.q: Which way is NOT allowed between two surahs?
options: Joining the end of the surah to the basmalah, then stopping
Stopping at the end of the surah and joining the basmalah to the next
quiz.why: It is not allowed, so that the basmalah is not taken as the end of the surah before it.

quiz.q: When starting in the middle of a surah, what about the basmalah?
quiz.why: In the middle of a surah, the reader may read the basmalah or leave it.

quiz.q: What are the ways between Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah?
options: Stop, pause briefly or join, without the basmalah
You cannot go from one to the other
quiz.why: At-Tawbah has no basmalah at its start, so the reader may stop, pause briefly (saktah) or join.

quiz.q: When does the reader say the isti'adhah quietly?
options: When reciting aloud with someone listening
quiz.why: It is said quietly in prayer and when reciting quietly, and aloud when reciting aloud with someone listening.

lessons.title: Vowel marks, tanween and sukun
lessons.lede: There are three vowel marks: fathah, dammah and kasrah. Tanween is a noon sakinah that is said but not written, and sukun means a letter has no vowel.

idea.lead: Every letter in the Quran either has one of the three vowel marks, fathah «ـَ», dammah «ـُ» or kasrah «ـِ», or has none, which is sukun. Tanween is an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun: it is said when joining but not written as a noon; it is marked by two vowel marks on the letter. Getting the vowels right is where tajweed starts, since saying one vowel instead of another is clear lahn.
idea.kidsLead: For fathah we open the mouth: «بَ». For dammah we round the lips: «بُ». For kasrah we lower the jaw: «بِ». Sukun means no vowel: «بْ». Tanween is two vowel marks, read with a little noon sound: «بٌ» sounds like «بُنْ».

how.text: A slanted line above the letter «ـَ»; the mouth opens.
A small waw above the letter «ـُ»; the lips round.
A slanted line below the letter «ـِ»; the jaw lowers.
In the Madinah Mushaf, a small head of khaa «ـۡ» above the letter; the letter is said without a vowel.
With fathah «ـً», dammah «ـٌ» or kasrah «ـٍ»; said as a noon sakinah at the end of a noun when joining.
Stop on tanween with fathah with an alif: «أَفۡوَاجَا»; on tanween with dammah or kasrah with sukun: «أَحَدْ», «خُسۡرْ».

idea.note: In the Madinah Mushaf, tanween is drawn as two marks side by side or stacked, depending on the letter after it: a hint of the rules of noon sakinah and tanween in level 2. The length of madd and ghunnah is measured in counts; one count is the time it takes to say one vowel.

ayat.findHint: Find the tanween and the sukun in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Sukun on the laam in «قُلۡ»
Tanween with dammah on the dal in «أَحَدٌ»
Sukun on the seen
Tanween with kasrah on the raa
Sukun on the faa
Tanween with fathah on the jeem, followed by an alif that is read when stopping

ayat.tip: In the Mushaf, sukun is a small head of khaa «ۡ» above the letter, as you can see in the ayahs above.

quiz.q: What are the three vowel marks?
quiz.why: The three vowel marks are fathah, dammah and kasrah; sukun means a letter has none of them.

quiz.q: How is tanween said?
options: As an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun
quiz.why: Tanween is an extra noon sakinah: it is said when joining, but not written as a noon.

quiz.q: What is the sign of sukun in the Madinah Mushaf?
quiz.why: Sukun is a small head of khaa. A small circle marks an extra letter that is not said.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «أَفۡوَاجٗا»?
quiz.why: When stopping, tanween with fathah becomes an alif.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «أَحَدٌ»?
quiz.why: When stopping, tanween with dammah or kasrah becomes a sukun.

quiz.q: In «خُسۡرٍ», what does the seen have?
quiz.why: The seen has the sukun sign «ۡ», and the raa after it has tanween with kasrah.

quiz.q: Is tanween written as a noon in the Mushaf?
options: No: it is said as a noon but not written as one
It is neither written nor said
It is written but not said
quiz.why: Tanween is written as two vowel marks, and said as a noon sakinah when joining.

lessons.title: Shaddah (doubled letters)
lessons.lede: A shaddah marks two of the same letter, the first with sukun and the second with a vowel, merged into one doubled letter.

formula.caption: the same letter with a vowel

idea.lead: A letter with a shaddah is two letters: the first has sukun, the second has a vowel, and the first is merged into the second. It is said by holding the tongue or lips on the point of articulation a little, then saying the letter with its vowel. The shaddah is a small head of seen «ـّ» above the letter, with the letter's vowel. So «رَبِّ» is said «رَبْ» then «بِ», joined.
idea.kidsLead: The shaddah is a small mark like the head of a seen «ـّ». A letter with a shaddah is read twice: once with sukun and once with its vowel, like «رَبِّ» = «رَبْ» + «بِ».

how.text: «رَبِّ» = «رَبْ» + «بِ»: the first baa has sukun and the second has kasrah, making one doubled baa.
A small head of seen «ـّ» above the letter, with a fathah or dammah above it, or a kasrah below it.
Hold the tongue or lips on the point of articulation a little, then say the letter with its vowel, without a break between the two.
With a shaddah, they always have ghunnah for two counts, as in «إِنَّ» and «ثُمَّ». Lesson 26 covers this.
The letter after a sun laam has a shaddah, as in «ٱلشَّمۡسِ». Lesson 15 covers this.

idea.note: Leaving out a shaddah is clear lahn, since it drops a letter from the word. A well-known example is reading «إِيَّاكَ» without the shaddah, which changes the meaning completely.

ayat.findHint: Find the letter with a shaddah and the letter with a sukun in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The yaa has a shaddah: two yaas, the first with sukun, the second with fathah
The 'ayn has a sukun, without a shaddah
The noon has a shaddah, with ghunnah
The 'ayn has a sukun
The baa has a shaddah: «رَبْ» then «بِ»
The laam has a sukun

ayat.tip: Compare: a letter with sukun is one letter with no vowel; a letter with a shaddah is two letters, the first with sukun.

quiz.q: What does a shaddah show?
options: Two letters: the first with sukun, the second with a vowel
A letter that is not said
quiz.why: A doubled letter is two of the same letter: the first, with sukun, is merged into the second, which has a vowel.

quiz.q: How is «رَبِّ» made up?
quiz.why: The doubled baa is two baas: the first with sukun «رَبْ», the second with kasrah «بِ».

quiz.q: What is the sign of shaddah?
quiz.why: The shaddah is a small head of seen «ـّ». The head of khaa is the sign of sukun.

quiz.q: Leaving out the shaddah in «إِيَّاكَ» is:
quiz.why: Leaving out the shaddah drops a letter and changes the meaning, so it is clear lahn.

quiz.q: When noon or meem has a shaddah, it always has:
quiz.why: Noon and meem with a shaddah are said with ghunnah for two counts.

quiz.q: In «إِيَّاكَ نَعۡبُدُ», which letter has a shaddah?
quiz.why: The yaa has a shaddah; the 'ayn has a sukun without a shaddah.

quiz.q: How is a letter with a shaddah said?
options: Holding the point of articulation a little, then with its vowel, without a break
quiz.why: The point of articulation is held a little, then the letter is said with its vowel: no break between the two, and not too light.

lessons.title: Points of articulation (makharij): the main areas
lessons.lede: A makhraj is where a letter comes from. There are seventeen, grouped into five main areas.

formula.caption: A hamzah with a vowel before it

idea.lead: Makhraj means "place of exit": as a term, it is where a letter comes from, which sets it apart from other letters. Ibn al-Jazari's choice is that there are seventeen makharij, grouped into five main areas: the open space (jawf), the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose (khayshum). To find a letter's makhraj, give it a sukun and put a hamzah with a vowel before it, as in «أَبْ» or «أَتْ»: where the sound stops is its makhraj.
idea.kidsLead: Every letter comes from a place: the open space inside the mouth and throat, the throat, the tongue, the lips or the nose. To find its place, say a hamzah with fathah before it and give it a sukun: «أَبْ», «أَتْ». Where the sound stops is its place.

how.text: The open space inside the throat and mouth: one makhraj, for the three madd letters.
Three makharij for six letters: ء ه, then ع ح, then غ خ.
Ten makharij for eighteen letters.
Two makharij for four letters: faa, then waw (when not a madd letter), baa and meem.
The back of the nose (khayshum), where ghunnah comes from.

idea.note: Scholars differ on the number: seventeen for al-Khalil and Ibn al-Jazari; sixteen for Sibawayh and ash-Shatibi, without the jawf; fourteen for al-Farra', who counts laam, noon and raa as one makhraj. The next lessons cover each main area.

quiz.q: How many makharij are there, by Ibn al-Jazari's choice?
quiz.why: Ibn al-Jazari's choice is seventeen makharij.

quiz.q: How many main areas are there?
quiz.why: Five: the jawf, the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose.

quiz.q: Which main area do the madd letters come from?
quiz.why: The three madd letters come from the jawf, the open space inside the throat and mouth.

quiz.q: How do you find a letter's makhraj?
options: Give it a sukun and put a hamzah with a vowel before it
quiz.why: As in «أَبْ»: where the sound stops is the letter's makhraj.

quiz.q: Which main area does ghunnah come from?
quiz.why: Ghunnah comes from the khayshum, at the back of the nose.

quiz.q: How many letters come from the tongue?
quiz.why: The tongue has ten makharij for eighteen letters, more than any other area.

lessons.title: The open space (jawf) and the madd letters
lessons.lede: The three madd letters come from the jawf: alif after fathah, waw with sukun after dammah, and yaa with sukun after kasrah.

idea.lead: The jawf is the open space inside the throat and mouth. The three madd letters come from it: alif with sukun after a fathah, waw with sukun after a dammah, and yaa with sukun after a kasrah. They are called the letters of the jawf, or of the air, because they do not stop at a fixed point like other letters: they end when the breath ends. All three come together in the word «نُوحِيهَا».
idea.kidsLead: There are three madd letters: alif after fathah «قَا», waw with sukun after dammah «قُو», and yaa with sukun after kasrah «قِي». They come from the open space inside the mouth and throat, and we stretch them for two counts.

how.text: Always has sukun, and the letter before it always has fathah, as in «قَالَ».
A madd letter when it has sukun and the letter before it has dammah, as in «يَقُولُ».

lessons.title: The makharij of the throat
lessons.lede: The throat has three makharij for six letters: its deepest part for hamzah and haa (ه), its middle for 'ayn and haa (ح), and its top for ghayn and khaa.

formula.caption: The deepest part and the middle

idea.lead: The throat has three parts, and two letters come from each. The deepest part, nearest the chest, gives hamzah and haa (ه). The middle gives 'ayn and haa (ح). The top, nearest the mouth, gives ghayn and khaa. Ibn al-Jazari says in his chapter on the makharij: «ثُمَّ لِأَقْصَى الحَلْقِ هَمْزٌ هَاءُ، ثُمَّ لِوَسْطِهِ فَعَيْنٌ حَاءُ، أَدْنَاهُ غَيْنٌ خَاؤُهَا» (then from the deepest part of the throat, hamzah and haa; from its middle, 'ayn and haa; from its top, ghayn and khaa).
idea.kidsLead: Six letters come from the throat: «ء ه» from deep down, near the chest; «ع ح» from the middle; and «غ خ» from the top, near the mouth. Put your hand on your neck and say: «أَعْ», «أَحْ», «أَخْ».

The part nearest the mouth: ghayn «أَغْ» and khaa «أَخْ».
These six are the throat letters of izhar: noon sakinah and tanween are said clearly before them. Lesson 17 covers this.
Say haa (ح) clearly, without turning it into haa (ه) or khaa; and say 'ayn clearly, without turning it into a hamzah.

idea.note: Sibawayh counted alif with hamzah and haa in the deepest part of the throat; Ibn al-Jazari's choice is that alif comes from the jawf, as in lesson 8. In the Mushaf, hamzah may be written on an alif «أ», under it «إ», or alone «ء»; it comes from the deepest part of the throat in every case.

lessons.title: The makharij of the tongue
lessons.lede: The tongue has more letters than any other area: ten makharij for eighteen letters, from its back, middle, sides and tip.

idea.lead: The tongue has ten makharij for eighteen letters, as Ibn al-Jazari sets out in his chapter on the makharij. From its back come qaaf, then kaaf a little lower; from its middle, jeem, sheen and yaa (when not a madd letter); from its side, daad, then laam; from its tip, noon, then raa, then taa (ط), dal and taa (ت), then saad, seen and zay, then dhaa (ظ), dhaal and thaa. Each comes from the tongue against what faces it: the roof of the mouth, the molars, the gums or the front teeth.
idea.kidsLead: Eighteen letters come from the tongue! From its back, qaaf and kaaf; from its middle, jeem, sheen and yaa; from its side, daad and laam; and from its tip, the rest, against the gums and the front teeth.

how.text: Qaaf, from the back of the tongue against the roof of the mouth; kaaf a little lower, towards the mouth.
Jeem, sheen and yaa (when not a madd letter), from the middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth.
Daad, from one or both sides of the tongue against the upper molars; laam, from the front of the side to the tip of the tongue.
Noon; then raa close to it, with the top of the tongue; then taa (ط), dal and taa (ت), against the roots of the upper front teeth.
Saad, seen and zay, from the tip of the tongue just above the lower front teeth; dhaa (ظ), dhaal and thaa, from the tip against the edges of the upper front teeth.

idea.note: Yaa comes from the middle of the tongue when it has a vowel, or a sukun after a fathah, as in «قُرَيۡشٍ»; the madd yaa comes from the jawf. Daad has the hardest makhraj of all the letters; it has a lesson with dhaa (ظ) in level 3. Al-Farra' counted laam, noon and raa as one makhraj.

lessons.title: The lips and the nose
lessons.lede: The lips have two makharij for four letters: faa, then waw, baa and meem. Ghunnah comes from the nose (khayshum).

formula.caption: The lower lip with the upper front teeth

idea.lead: The lips have two makharij. The first is the inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth: faa comes from it. The second is between the lips: waw (when not a madd letter), with the lips rounded and a little open, and baa and meem, with the lips closed. The khayshum is the back of the nose: ghunnah comes from it, a sound that goes with noon and meem. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَمِنْ بَطْنِ الشَّفَهْ فَالفَا مَعَ اطْرَافِ الثَّنَايَا المُشْرِفَهْ، لِلشَّفَتَيْنِ الوَاوُ بَاءٌ مِيمُ، وَغُنَّةٌ مَخْرَجُهَا الخَيْشُومُ» (from the inside of the lip, faa, with the edges of the upper front teeth; from the two lips, waw, baa and meem; and ghunnah, whose makhraj is the khayshum).
idea.kidsLead: For faa, we put our top teeth on the lower lip: «أَفْ». For baa and meem, we close the lips: «أَبْ», «أَمْ». For waw, we round the lips: «أَوْ». Ghunnah is a sound from the nose that goes with noon and meem: hold your nose and say «أَمْ» to feel it.

how.text: From the inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth: «أَفْ».
When not a madd letter: from between the lips, rounded and a little open: «أَوْ».
From between the lips, closed; baa closes them more firmly: «أَبْ», «أَمْ».
The back of the nose: the ghunnah of noon and meem comes from it; holding the nose stops it.
It is strongest in noon and meem with a shaddah. Lesson 26 covers it.

idea.note: The madd waw, as in «يَقُولُ», comes from the jawf, not the lips, as in lesson 8. Ibn al-Jazari states that noon and meem come from the khayshum in ikhfa' and in idgham with ghunnah. Common mistakes: saying faa from between the lips, or pressing on meem until it sounds like baa.

lessons.title: Letters that sound alike
lessons.lede: Some letters are close in makhraj or in sound, so beginners mix them up. Saying one instead of another is clear lahn, and it can change the meaning.

idea.lead: A beginner's most common mistake is saying one letter instead of another that sounds like it: «عَصَى» (he disobeyed) is not «عَسَى» (perhaps), and «التِّين» (figs) is not «الطِّين» (clay). There are several kinds. A light and a heavy letter from the same or a nearby makhraj: seen and saad, taa (ت) and taa (ط), dhaal and dhaa (ظ), kaaf and qaaf. Throat letters close to each other: hamzah and 'ayn, haa (ه) and haa (ح). Letters from the tip of the tongue and the front teeth: thaa and seen, dhaal and zay. What sets them apart is their makhraj or their characteristics (sifat).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters sound alike, so we listen carefully: «س» is light and «ص» is full; «ت» is light and «ط» is full; «ك» is light and «ق» comes from the back of the tongue. If we say one instead of the other, the meaning changes: «عَصَى» is not «عَسَى».

how.text: The same makhraj: saad is heavy and covered, seen is light. «عَصَى» is not «عَسَى».
The same makhraj: taa (ط) is heavy and covered, taa (ت) is light. «التِّين» is not «الطِّين».
Dhaal is light and dhaa (ظ) is heavy, from the same makhraj. Daad comes from the side of the tongue: do not say it as dhaa (ظ) or as a heavy dal.
Qaaf comes from deeper in the back of the tongue than kaaf, and it is heavy; kaaf is light.
'Ayn and haa (ح) come from the middle of the throat; hamzah and haa (ه) from its deepest part. Do not say 'ayn as a hamzah, or haa (ح) as haa (ه).
For thaa and dhaal, the tip of the tongue touches the edges of the upper front teeth; seen and zay come from just above the lower front teeth, with a whistle.

idea.note: Two letters from the same makhraj differ in their characteristics (sifat): lesson 13 and lessons 33–37 cover them. Daad and dhaa (ظ) have their own lesson in level 3, since mistakes in them are so common.

lessons.title: Characteristics of the letters (sifat): an introduction
lessons.lede: A sifah is the way a letter comes out of its makhraj. The makhraj fixes where a letter comes from; its sifat set it apart from the letters that share that makhraj.

idea.lead: In Arabic, a sifah is a quality something has. As a term, it is the way a letter comes out of its makhraj: whether the breath flows or stops, whether the sound flows or stops, whether the tongue rises or stays low, and so on. Ibn al-Jazari lists seventeen in his chapter on the sifat: five with opposites, making ten, and seven without. He says: «صِفَاتُهَا جَهْرٌ وَرِخْوٌ مُسْتَفِلْ، مُنْفَتِحٌ مُصْمَتَةٌ وَالضِّدَّ قُلْ» (its sifat are jahr, rikhwah, istifal, infitah and ismat; and name their opposites).
idea.kidsLead: Every letter has a place it comes from, and qualities that make its sound different: strong or weak, with the breath flowing or held, full or light. «ت», «د» and «ط» come from the same place, but their qualities make each one a different letter.

how.text: To tell apart letters that share a makhraj: taa (ت), dal and taa (ط) come from one makhraj and differ by their sifat.
To say each letter well, and to know the strong letters from the weak, giving each its due.
Five: hams (breath flows) and jahr; shiddah (sound stops) and rikhawah, with tawassut between them; isti'la' (tongue rises) and istifal; itbaq (tongue covers) and infitah; idhlaq and ismat.
Seven: safir (whistle), qalqalah, leen, inhiraf, takrir (rolling), tafashshi (spreading) and istitalah (lengthening).
Taa (ت) is mahmus, shadid, mustafil, munfatih and musmat; taa (ط) is majhur, shadid, musta'li, mutbaq, musmat and has qalqalah. That is why taa (ط) is heavy.

idea.note: Every letter has five sifat from the pairs with opposites, one from each pair, and may have some of those without opposites too. Those who count seventeen do not count tawassut, between shiddah and rikhawah, separately; others do. Level 3 covers each sifah (lessons 33–37).

quiz.q: What is the main use of knowing the sifat?

quiz.why: Only their sifat set apart letters that come from the same makhraj.

quiz.why: Seventeen: ten in five pairs of opposites, and seven without opposites.

quiz.why: Qalqalah is one of the seven sifat without an opposite.

quiz.q: Why is taa (ط) heavy and taa (ت) light?
quiz.why: They share a makhraj; the difference is in their sifat: taa (ط) is musta'li and mutbaq, taa (ت) is mustafil and munfatih.

lessons.title: Qalqalah (echo) and its degrees
lessons.lede: Qalqalah is a bounce in the makhraj when one of the letters of «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ» has a sukun, so that a strong echo is heard.

idea.lead: In Arabic, qalqalah means shaking. As a term, it is a bounce in the makhraj when a letter with sukun is said, so that a strong echo is heard. Its five letters come together in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ». They bounce because each has both jahr and shiddah: jahr holds the breath and shiddah holds the sound, so a letter with sukun needs its makhraj to open to be heard. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَبَيِّنَنْ مُقَلْقَلًا إِنْ سَكَنَا، وَإِنْ يَكُنْ فِي الوَقْفِ كَانَ أَبْيَنَا» (make the qalqalah letter clear when it has sukun; when stopping, it is clearer still).
idea.kidsLead: There are five qalqalah letters, which we gather in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ». When one of them has a sukun, we read it with a little bounce, as if it jumps: «يَلِدْ», «ٱقْرَأْ». When we stop on it, the bounce is clearer: «ٱلْفَلَقْ».

how.text: Five: qaaf, taa (ط), baa, jeem and dal, gathered in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ».
The letter must have a sukun; with a vowel, there is no qalqalah.
When the letter has a sukun in the middle of the reading, as in «يَلِدۡ» and «ٱقۡرَأۡ».

lessons.title: The sun and moon laam
lessons.lede: The laam of «ال» ("the") is said clearly before fourteen letters, called the moon letters, and merges into the other fourteen, called the sun letters.

idea.lead: The laam of «ال» ("the") is an extra laam with sukun added to a noun. It has two cases, depending on the letter after it. Before the moon letters, the fourteen gathered in «ابْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ», it is said clearly, with sukun, as in «ٱلۡقَمَرِ» (the moon): this is izhar. Before the sun letters, the other fourteen, it is not said, and the letter after it is doubled, as in «ٱلشَّمۡسِ» (the sun): this is idgham. The author of Tuhfat al-Atfal says: «لِلَامِ أَلْ حَالَانِ قَبْلَ الأَحْرُفِ، أُولَاهُمَا إِظْهَارُهَا فَلْتَعْرِفِ» (the laam of al has two cases before the letters; the first is izhar, so know it).
idea.kidsLead: «ال» at the start of a word has two cases. With the moon letters, we say the laam clearly: «ٱلْقَمَر». With the sun letters, we hide the laam and double the letter after it: «ٱلشَّمْس», just as the sun's light hides the stars.

how.text: Fourteen letters, gathered in «ابْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ»: the laam before them is said, with sukun: «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ».
The other fourteen, «ط ث ص ر ت ض ذ ن د س ظ ز ش ل»: the laam merges into them: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».
In the Mushaf, the moon laam has a sukun; the sun laam has no mark, and the letter after it has a shaddah.
The hamzah of «ال» is a joining hamzah: it is said with fathah when starting, and dropped when joining, as in «وَٱلشَّمۡسِ».
This rule is only for the laam of «ال»: a laam that belongs to the word is always said, as in «أَلۡسِنَتُهُمۡ» and «قُلۡ نَعَمۡ».

idea.note: The names come from the two words: the moon, «ٱلۡقَمَرِ», where the laam is said, and the sun, «ٱلشَّمۡسِ», where it merges. Laam is itself a sun letter: in «ٱللَّيۡلِ», the laam of «ال» merges into the laam after it.

lessons.title: Noon sakinah and tanween: an introduction
lessons.lede: A noon sakinah is a noon with no vowel; tanween is an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun. They have four rules, depending on the letter after them.

idea.lead: A noon sakinah is a noon with no vowel. It is both said and written, and it stays when joining and when stopping. It comes in nouns, verbs and particles, in the middle or at the end of a word, as in «أَنۡعَمۡتَ» and «مِنۡ». Tanween is an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun: it is said but not written as a noon, and it stays when joining but drops when stopping. They have four rules, depending on the letter after them. The author of Tuhfat al-Atfal says: «لِلنُّونِ إِنْ تَسْكُنْ وَلِلتَّنْوِينِ، أَرْبَعُ أَحْكَامٍ فَخُذْ تَبْيِينِي» (noon sakinah and tanween have four rules, so take my explanation).
idea.kidsLead: A noon sakinah is a noon with a sukun «نْ». Tanween is two vowel marks with a little noon sound «ـٌ». We look at the letter after them to know how to read them: say the noon clearly, merge it into the next letter, turn it into a meem, or hide it.

how.text: A noon sakinah is written and stays when stopping; it comes in nouns, verbs and particles. Tanween is not written as a noon, drops when stopping, and comes only at the end of a noun.
Before the six throat letters «ء ه ع ح غ خ». Lesson 17.
Into the six letters of «يَرْمَلُونَ»: with ghunnah into «يَنْمُو», without ghunnah into laam and raa. Lessons 18 and 19.
Before baa alone. Lesson 20.
Before the other fifteen letters. Lesson 21.

idea.note: The Mushaf's marks show the rule: a sukun on the noon, and stacked tanween marks, for izhar; no sukun and a shaddah on the next letter for full idgham; no sukun and no shaddah for partial idgham and ikhfa'; a small meem for iqlab. In ikhfa' and idgham, tanween is written as two marks one after the other.

lessons.title: Izhar (clear)
lessons.lede: When one of the six throat letters comes after a noon sakinah or tanween, the noon is said clearly from its makhraj, without extra ghunnah.

idea.lead: In Arabic, izhar means making clear. As a term, it is saying each letter from its makhraj, with no extra ghunnah in the letter made clear. Its letters are six: hamzah, haa (ه), 'ayn, haa (ح), ghayn and khaa. It is called "of the throat" because they come from the throat. It happens because the makhraj of noon, at the tip of the tongue, is far from the throat letters. The author of the Tuhfah says: «فَالأَوَّلُ الإِظْهَارُ قَبْلَ أَحْرُفِ، لِلْحَلْقِ سِتٌّ رُتِّبَتْ فَلْتَعْرِفِ» (the first is izhar, before the six throat letters, in their order, so know them).
idea.kidsLead: When a noon sakinah or tanween comes before one of the six throat letters «ء ه ع ح غ خ», we say the noon clearly, without stretching its sound: «مَنْ أَعْطَى», «نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ».

how.text: «ء ه ع ح غ خ»: the first letters of the words in «أَخِي هَاكَ عِلْمًا حَازَهُ غَيْرُ خَاسِرِ».
The tip of the tongue touches the makhraj of noon, so the noon is clear; then move to the throat letter without a pause.
Do not stretch it: the noon keeps only its own light ghunnah.
The makhraj of noon, at the tip of the tongue, is far from the throat letters.
In one word: «يَنۡهَىٰ»; across two words: «مَنۡ أَعۡطَىٰ»; with tanween: «نَارٌ حَامِيَةُۢ».

idea.note: Common mistakes: giving the clear noon a qalqalah, pausing on it, or stretching its ghunnah. Hafs says the noon clearly before ghayn and khaa, as before the other throat letters; some other riwayahs hide it before those two.

lessons.title: Idgham with ghunnah
lessons.lede: When a letter of «يَنْمُو» begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, the noon merges into it, with ghunnah for two counts.

idea.lead: In Arabic, idgham means putting one thing into another. As a term, it is a letter with sukun meeting a letter with a vowel, so that the two become one doubled letter, like the second. The letters of idgham for noon sakinah and tanween are six, gathered in «يَرْمَلُونَ»; four of them, gathered in «يَنْمُو», take ghunnah. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِسِتَّةٍ أَتَتْ، فِي يَرْمَلُونَ عِنْدَهُمْ قَدْ ثَبَتَتْ، لَكِنَّهَا قِسْمَانِ قِسْمٌ يُدْغَمَا، فِيهِ بِغُنَّةٍ بِيَنْمُو عُلِمَا» (the second is idgham, into six letters, fixed in «يَرْمَلُونَ»; but they are of two kinds: one takes idgham with ghunnah, known as «يَنْمُو»).
idea.kidsLead: When a letter of «يَنْمُو» begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, we merge the noon into that letter and keep the ghunnah sound from the nose for two counts: «مَن يَعْمَلْ» is read «مَيَّعْمَلْ».

how.text: Yaa, noon, meem and waw, gathered in «يَنْمُو».
Into noon and meem: the noon goes completely, and the ghunnah is that of the letter merged into: «مِن نِّعۡمَةٖ», «مِّن مَّسَدِۭ».
Into yaa and waw: the noon itself goes, but its ghunnah stays: «مَن يَعۡمَلۡ», «يَوۡمَئِذٖ وَاجِفَةٌ».
Two counts in all of them.
It must be across two words. When noon and yaa or waw meet in one word, the noon is said clearly: «ٱلدُّنۡيَا», «بُنۡيَٰنٞ», «صِنۡوَانٞ» and «قِنۡوَانٞ». This is called absolute izhar.

idea.note: Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, says the noon clearly in «يسٓ ۝ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ» and «نٓۚ وَٱلۡقَلَمِ», even though waw comes after it. In the Mushaf, the noon has no sukun; the next letter has a shaddah in full idgham, and none in partial idgham.

lessons.title: Idgham without ghunnah
lessons.lede: When laam or raa begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, the noon merges into it completely, without ghunnah.

idea.lead: Idgham without ghunnah is merging a noon sakinah or tanween into laam or raa: the noon goes completely, with its ghunnah, and the next letter is said doubled, without ghunnah. It is called full because the noon and its ghunnah both go. It happens because the makhraj of noon is close to those of laam and raa. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِغَيْرِ غُنَّهْ، فِي اللَّامِ وَالرَّا ثُمَّ كَرِّرَنَّهْ» (the second is idgham without ghunnah, into laam and raa; and roll the raa).
idea.kidsLead: When laam or raa begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, we do not say the noon at all, and there is no ghunnah: we double the laam or raa. «وَيْلٌ لِّكُلِّ» is read «وَيْلُلِّكُلِّ».

how.text: Laam and raa.
The noon is not said, and the next letter is doubled: «وَيۡلٞ لِّكُلِّ» is read «وَيۡلُلِّكُلِّ».
There is none: the idgham is full.
It happens only across two words, as in «مِن رَّبِّهِمۡ» and «غَفُورٞ رَّحِيمٞ».
In the Mushaf, the noon has no sukun, and the laam or raa after it has a shaddah.

Idgham without ghunnah is how Hafs reads by way of ash-Shatibiyyah; by other ways there is also a reading with ghunnah into laam and raa.

lessons.title: Meem sakinah: an introduction
lessons.lede: A meem sakinah is a meem with no vowel. It has three rules: ikhfa' before baa, idgham into meem, and izhar before every other letter.

idea.lead: A meem sakinah is a meem with no vowel. It stays when joining and when stopping, and comes in the middle or at the end of a word, in nouns, verbs and particles. Any letter can come after it except the madd letters. It has three rules, depending on the letter after it. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالمِيمُ إِنْ تَسْكُنْ تَجِي قَبْلَ الهِجَا، لَا أَلِفٍ لَيِّنَةٍ لِذِي الحِجَا، أَحْكَامُهَا ثَلَاثَةٌ لِمَنْ ضَبَطْ، إِخْفَاءٌ ادْغَامٌ وَإِظْهَارٌ فَقَطْ» (meem sakinah comes before the letters, but not before a soft alif; its rules are three: ikhfa', idgham and izhar, no more).

how.text: Before baa: ikhfa' with the lips. Lesson 23.

In the Mushaf, the meem has a sukun for izhar, and none for ikhfa' and idgham; in idgham, the meem after it has a shaddah.

lessons.lede: Noon and meem with a shaddah are said with full ghunnah for two counts; each is called a doubled letter of ghunnah.

idea.lead: Ghunnah is a nasal sound built into noon and meem. It comes from the khayshum, and the tongue plays no part in it. When noon or meem has a shaddah, its ghunnah must be said for two counts, when joining and when stopping, in the middle or at the end of a word, as in «إِنَّ» and «ثُمَّ». The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَغُنَّ مِيمًا ثُمَّ نُونًا شُدِّدَا، وَسَمِّ كُلًّا حَرْفَ غُنَّةٍ بَدَا» (give ghunnah to meem and noon with a shaddah, and call each a letter of ghunnah).

lessons.title: Madd: its meaning, letters and causes
lessons.lede: Madd is stretching the sound of a madd letter. The original madd is two counts; a secondary madd is longer, because of a hamzah or a sukun.

idea.lead: In Arabic, madd means increase. As a term, it is stretching the sound of a madd letter; its opposite is qasr, saying the madd letter with no extra length. It is of two kinds. The original madd, also called natural, is needed for the letter to exist at all and does not depend on any cause; it lasts two counts. A secondary madd is longer than the natural one, because of a hamzah or a sukun. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالمَدُّ أَصْلِيٌّ وَفَرْعِيٌّ لَهُ، وَسَمِّ أَوَّلًا طَبِيعِيًّا وَهُو، مَا لَا تَوَقُّفٌ لَهُ عَلَى سَبَبْ، وَلَا بِدُونِهِ الحُرُوفُ تُجْتَلَبْ» (madd is original or secondary; call the first natural: it does not depend on a cause, and without it the letters cannot be said).
idea.kidsLead: Madd means stretching the sound of a madd letter: alif, waw or yaa. The shortest is two counts, as in «قَالَ». When a hamzah or a sukun comes after the madd letter, we stretch it longer, as in «جَآءَ».

how.text: Alif after fathah, waw with sukun after dammah, yaa with sukun after kasrah, as in lesson 8.
Waw and yaa with sukun after fathah, as in «خَوۡفٍ»; they are stretched only when stopping. Lesson 31.
Two counts, with no cause: «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ». Lesson 28.
A hamzah after the madd letter, in one word «جَآءَ» or the next word «إِنَّآ أَنزَلۡنَٰهُ»: lesson 29. Or a hamzah before it «ءَامَنُواْ»: lesson 32.
A fixed sukun after the madd letter «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ»: lesson 30. Or a sukun for stopping «ٱلرَّحِيمِ»: lesson 31.

idea.note: One count is the time it takes to say one vowel, about the time to fold or unfold a finger. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, reads the joined and separated madd for four or five counts, and the necessary madd for six; their lessons give the details.

lessons.title: Natural madd (madd tabi'i)
lessons.lede: The natural madd is stretching a madd letter for two counts, when no hamzah or sukun comes after it.

formula.caption: no hamzah or sukun after it

idea.lead: The natural madd is the original madd: a madd letter cannot be said without it, and it does not depend on a hamzah or a sukun. It lasts two counts, no more and no less. It is called natural because someone with a sound natural ear neither shortens it nor stretches it. The small alif over a letter, as in «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ», counts too: it is stretched like an alif.
idea.kidsLead: The natural madd is the shortest madd: we stretch the madd letter for just two counts, as in «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ». The small alif over a letter is also stretched for two counts: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».

how.text: Two counts, no more and no less: «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ».
The small alif «ـٰ» over a letter is stretched for two counts, like an alif: «ذَٰلِكَ», «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».
The letters at the start of surahs that are said with two letters, gathered in «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ»: «ح ي ط ه ر». «طه» is read «طَا هَا».
It is two counts when you stop on the madd letter itself, as when stopping on «وَٱلضُّحَىٰ».
When a madd letter ends a word and a letter with sukun begins the next, the madd drops when joining: «قَالُواْ ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» is read «قَالُلۡحَمۡدُ».

idea.note: A common beginner's mistake is cutting the natural madd until it becomes a vowel, or stretching it past two counts. The minor silah and the 'iwad madd have the same length as the natural madd; lesson 32 covers them.

lessons.title: Joined and separated madd
lessons.lede: When a hamzah follows a madd letter in the same word, it is the joined madd, which is required; when the hamzah begins the next word, it is the separated madd, which is allowed. Hafs gives both four or five counts.

idea.lead: The joined (muttasil) madd is a madd letter followed by a hamzah in the same word, as in «جَآءَ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ» and «سُوٓءَ». It is required, since all the reciters agree on stretching it beyond the natural madd. The separated (munfasil) madd is a madd letter ending one word and a hamzah beginning the next, as in «بِمَآ أُنزِلَ» and «قُوٓاْ أَنفُسَكُمۡ». It is allowed, since some reciters shorten it. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَوَاجِبٌ إِنْ جَاءَ قَبْلَ هَمْزَةِ، مُتَّصِلًا إِنْ جُمِعَا بِكِلْمَةِ، وَجَائِزٌ إِذَا أَتَى مُنْفَصِلَا» (it is required when it comes before a hamzah, joined, in one word; and allowed when it comes separated).
idea.kidsLead: When a hamzah comes after a madd letter, we stretch longer than two counts: four or five. If the hamzah is in the same word «جَآءَ», the madd is joined; if it is in the next word «إِنَّآ أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ», it is separated.

how.text: The madd letter and the hamzah are in one word: «جَآءَ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», «سُوٓءَ».
Required. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts.
The madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next: «بِمَآ أُنزِلَ», «قُوٓاْ أَنفُسَكُمۡ», «فِيٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡ».
Allowed. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts, like the joined madd.
Within one recitation, give them the same length: four for both, or five for both.
When you stop on a joined madd whose hamzah ends the word, as in «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», four, five or six counts are allowed.

idea.note: Shortening the separated madd to two counts comes from Hafs by way of Tayyibat an-Nashr, not by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, which this course follows. The madd sign «ـٓ» over a madd letter in the Mushaf marks a madd longer than the natural one, in both the joined and the separated madd.

lessons.title: Madd lazim, in words and in letters
lessons.lede: A madd letter followed by a fixed sukun, in a word or in the name of a letter: always six counts.

idea.lead: The necessary (lazim) madd is a madd letter followed by a fixed sukun, there both when joining and when stopping. It is called necessary because its cause is always there, and because all the reciters agree on six counts. Ibn al-Jazari says: «فَلَازِمٌ إِنْ جَاءَ بَعْدَ حَرْفِ مَدّْ، سَاكِنُ حَالَيْنِ وَبِالطُّولِ يُمَدّْ» (it is necessary when, after a madd letter, comes a sukun in both states; it is stretched long). It has four kinds: heavy in a word, light in a word, heavy in a letter, and light in a letter. The author of the Tuhfah says: «أَقْسَامُ لَازِمٍ لَدَيْهِمْ أَرْبَعَهْ، وَتِلْكَ كِلْمِيٌّ وَحَرْفِيٌّ مَعَهْ، كِلَاهُمَا مُخَفَّفٌ مُثَقَّلُ، فَهَذِهِ أَرْبَعَةٌ تُفَصَّلُ» (the necessary madd has four kinds: in a word and in a letter, each light or heavy).
idea.kidsLead: When a letter with sukun or a shaddah comes after a madd letter in the same word, we stretch it long: six counts, as in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ». Some letters at the start of surahs too: «الٓمٓ» is read «أَلِفْ لَآمْ مِيمْ».

how.text: A madd letter and a doubled letter after it, in one word: «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», «ٱلصَّآخَّةُ», «دَآبَّةٖ».
A madd letter and a sukun without idgham after it, in one word: in the Quran, «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ», twice in Yunus (51 and 91).
At the start of surahs: each letter whose name has three letters with a madd letter in the middle, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ»: «ن ق ص ع س ل ك م».
When the end of the letter merges into the next: «الٓمٓ» is read «لَآمِّيمْ», so the laam is heavy.
When it does not merge: «قٓ», «نٓ», «صٓ», and the meem of «الٓمٓ».
In «كٓهيعٓصٓ» and «حمٓ ۝ عٓسٓقٓ», 'ayn is stretched four or six counts, six being preferred, since its yaa is a leen letter, not a madd letter.

idea.note: The madd in «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ» (Al-An'am 143 and 144), «ءَآللَّهُ» (Yunus 59, An-Naml 59) and «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» is called the madd of distinction, since it tells a question apart from a statement. Hafs has two ways in these words: turning the second hamzah into an alif and stretching it six counts, or easing it (tas-hil) between hamzah and alif, without madd. Learn the easing from a teacher.

lessons.title: Madd 'arid and madd al-leen
lessons.lede: When you stop on a word with a madd or leen letter before its last letter, the last letter takes a sukun for the stop, and the madd may be two, four or six counts.

idea.lead: The madd for stopping (al-'arid lis-sukun) is a madd letter followed by a letter that takes a sukun because you stop, as when stopping on «ٱلرَّحِيمِ», «نَسۡتَعِينُ» and «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ». The leen madd is a waw or yaa with sukun after a fathah, followed by a letter that takes a sukun for the stop, as in «خَوۡفِۭ» and «ٱلۡبَيۡتِ». When stopping, both may be two counts (qasr), four (tawassut) or six (tul). When the word is joined to the next, the sukun goes, and so does the madd. Ibn al-Jazari says: «أَوْ عَرَضَ السُّكُونُ وَقْفًا مُسْجَلَا» (or when the sukun comes for stopping, in every case).
idea.kidsLead: When we stop at the end of an ayah on a word with a madd letter before its last letter, like «ٱلرَّحِيمْ», we may stretch two, four or six counts. The same goes for «خَوْفْ» and «ٱلْبَيْتْ». When we join the word to the next, we do not stretch more.

how.text: A madd letter followed by a letter with sukun for the stop: «ٱلرَّحِيمۡ», «نَسۡتَعِينۡ», «يَعۡلَمُونۡ».
A waw or yaa with sukun after a fathah, followed by a letter with sukun for the stop: «خَوۡفۡ», «ٱلۡبَيۡتۡ».
Two, four or six counts when stopping; the leen letter is not stretched at all when joining.
Whatever length you choose for the madd for stopping, keep it through the recitation; and do not stretch the leen madd more than the madd for stopping when both come.
When you stop with rawm, saying part of the vowel, only two counts are allowed, since the sukun is not complete. Level 3 covers rawm.

idea.note: When a joined madd comes before the letter you stop on, as in «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», lesson 29 applies: four, five or six counts. When the madd letter is itself the last letter you stop on, as in «وَٱلضُّحَىٰ», it is a natural madd.

lessons.title: Madd badal, silah and 'iwad
lessons.lede: Three madds that Hafs mostly gives two counts: badal, a hamzah before a madd letter; silah, a waw or yaa after the pronoun haa; and 'iwad, an alif in place of tanween with fathah when stopping.

formula.caption: A hamzah before the madd letter
An alif in place of tanween

idea.lead: The badal madd is a hamzah coming before a madd letter in a word, as in «ءَامَنُواْ», «أُوتُواْ» and «إِيمَٰنٗا». It is called badal (replacement) because the madd letter usually replaces a hamzah: «ءَامَنَ» was «أَأْمَنَ». The silah madd is joining the pronoun haa ("him", "it") to a waw when it has a dammah, or to a yaa when it has a kasrah, when it comes between two letters with vowels, as in «إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ» and «بِهِۦ». The 'iwad madd is stopping on tanween with fathah with an alif: «تَوَّابَۢا» is read «تَوَّابَا».
idea.kidsLead: Badal: a hamzah before a madd letter, «ءَامَنُوا»; we stretch it two counts. Silah: a small waw or small yaa after the haa, «إِنَّهُۥ»; we read it for two counts. 'Iwad: we stop on tanween with fathah with an alif, «تَوَّابَا», for two counts.

how.text: A hamzah before the madd letter: «ءَامَنُواْ», «أُوتُواْ», «إِيمَٰنٗا». Hafs gives it two counts only.
A silah with no hamzah after it: «إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ», «بِهِۦ بَصِيرًا»; two counts.
A silah with a hamzah after it: «مَالَهُۥٓ أَخۡلَدَهُۥ». It follows the separated madd: four or five counts for Hafs.
When a letter with sukun comes after the haa «لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُ», or before it «مِنۡهُ», or when you stop on it.
Stopping on tanween with fathah with an alif, for two counts: «عَلِيمٗا» is read «عَلِيمَا». Not on taa marbutah: you stop on «رَحۡمَةٗ» with a haa.

idea.note: Hafs has special readings for the pronoun haa: he joins it in «فِيهِۦ مُهَانًا» (Al-Furqan 69), though a letter with sukun comes before it; he does not join it in «يَرۡضَهُ لَكُمۡ» (Az-Zumar 7), reading a dammah only; he gives it a sukun in «أَرۡجِهۡ» (Al-A'raf 111, Ash-Shu'ara 36) and «فَأَلۡقِهۡ» (An-Naml 28); and he gives it a dammah in «عَلَيۡهُ ٱللَّهَ» (Al-Fath 10) and «أَنسَىٰنِيهُ» (Al-Kahf 63).

lessons.title: Hams and jahr (whispered and voiced)
lessons.lede: Hams is the breath flowing with a letter, because it presses lightly on its makhraj; its ten letters are gathered in «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ». Jahr is its opposite.

idea.lead: In Arabic, hams means quietness. As a term, it is the breath flowing as a letter is said, because the letter presses lightly on its makhraj. Its ten letters are gathered in «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ». Jahr means openness: as a term, the breath being held as a letter is said, because the letter presses firmly on its makhraj. Its letters are the other nineteen. Ibn al-Jazari says: «مَهْمُوسُهَا فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتْ» (its whispered letters are «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتْ»).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters come out with a breath, like a whisper: «سْ», «شْ», «فْ». There are ten, gathered in «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ». The other letters have a strong sound that holds the breath, like «دْ» and «عْ». Put your hand in front of your mouth and say «أَسْ», then «أَزْ»: you feel the air in the first.

how.text: Faa, haa (ح), thaa, haa (ه), sheen, khaa, saad, seen, kaaf and taa: «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ».
Nineteen letters: all the others, such as dal, 'ayn and meem.
Give the letter a sukun after a hamzah: in «أَسْ» the breath flows; in «أَزْ» it is held, though both come from one makhraj.
Whispered and shadid: the sound stops, then a little breath comes out, with no exaggeration and no qalqalah: «وَٱتۡلُ», «يُدۡرِكۡكُمُ».
It tells apart letters that share a makhraj, such as whispered taa (ت) and voiced dal, or seen and zay.

idea.note: Hams is clearest in a letter with sukun. Mistakes: overdoing the hams until the letter whistles or puffs, or losing it so that taa and kaaf with sukun bounce as if they were qalqalah letters.

lessons.title: Shiddah, rakhawah and tawassut
lessons.lede: Shiddah is the sound being held with a letter; its letters are «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ». Rakhawah is the sound flowing. Tawassut is in between; its letters are «لِنْ عُمَرْ».

idea.lead: In Arabic, shiddah means strength. As a term, it is the sound being held as a letter is said, because it presses on its makhraj with full strength. Its eight letters are gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ». Rakhawah means softness: the sound flowing with the letter, because it presses lightly. Tawassut is in between: the sound is neither fully held nor fully flowing. Its five letters are gathered in «لِنْ عُمَرْ». Ibn al-Jazari says: «شَدِيدُهَا لَفْظُ أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ، وَبَيْنَ رِخْوٍ وَالشَّدِيدِ لِنْ عُمَرْ» (its shadid letters are the words «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ», and between rikhw and shadid are «لِنْ عُمَرْ»).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters stop their sound suddenly, like «أَدْ» and «أَقْ»: there are eight, gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ». Some let their sound go on, like «أَسْ» and «أَشْ». Five are in the middle, their sound going on a little: «لِنْ عُمَرْ».

how.text: Eight letters: hamzah, jeem, dal, qaaf, taa (ط), baa, kaaf and taa (ت), gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ».
Five letters: laam, noon, 'ayn, meem and raa, gathered in «لِنْ عُمَرْ».
Sixteen letters: all the others, such as seen, sheen and faa.
Give the letter a sukun after a hamzah: in «أَدْ» the sound stops; in «أَسْ» it goes on; in «أَلْ» it goes on a little, then stops.
Shiddah holds the sound; jahr holds the breath. So kaaf and taa are shadid and whispered: the sound is held while the breath flows.

idea.note: The letters with both jahr and shiddah are the qalqalah letters «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ», since both breath and sound are held. Mistakes: letting the sound of a shadid letter with sukun go on, cutting off the sound of a rikhw letter, or drawing out the letters of tawassut.

lessons.title: Isti'la', istifal, itbaq and infitah
lessons.lede: Isti'la' is the back of the tongue rising to the palate; its letters are «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ». Itbaq is the tongue covering the palate; its letters are «ص ض ط ظ». Their opposites are istifal and infitah.

idea.lead: In Arabic, isti'la' means rising. As a term, it is the back of the tongue rising to the roof of the mouth as a letter is said. Its seven letters are gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ». Its opposite, istifal, is the tongue staying low, in all the other letters. Itbaq means covering: as a term, part of the tongue pressing against the roof of the mouth, with the sound closed in between. Its four letters are saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ); its opposite is infitah (openness). Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَسَبْعُ عُلْوٍ خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ حَصَرْ، وَصَادُ ضَادٌ طَاءُ ظَاءٌ مُطْبَقَهْ» (seven rise, gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ»; and saad, daad, taa and dhaa are covered).
idea.kidsLead: For seven letters we lift the back of the tongue to the roof of the mouth, so their sound is full: «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ». For four of them we press the tongue against the roof even more, so they are stronger: «ص ض ط ظ».

how.text: Seven letters: khaa, saad, daad, ghayn, taa (ط), qaaf and dhaa (ظ), gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ».
Four of them: saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ), the heaviest letters of all.
Every covered letter is raised, but not every raised letter is covered: khaa, ghayn and qaaf are raised and open.
Twenty-two letters: all the others. They are light, except raa, laam and alif in some cases.
Isti'la' makes a letter heavy, and itbaq makes it heavier still: taa (ط) is heavier than qaaf.

idea.note: Taa (ط) has the most isti'la' and itbaq, then daad, then saad, then dhaa (ظ). Mistakes: making the raised letters light, especially before a yaa or a kasrah, as in «قِيلَ» and «خِيفَةٗ»; or making the low letters before them heavy.

lessons.title: Idhlaq and ismat
lessons.lede: Idhlaq is a letter being light and quick to say, because it comes from the tip of the tongue or the lips; its six letters are gathered in «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ». Ismat is its opposite.

idea.lead: In Arabic, idhlaq means a sharp, fluent tongue. As a term, it is a letter being light and quick to say, because it comes from the tip of the tongue or from the lip. Its six letters are gathered in «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ»: faa, raa, meem, noon, laam and baa. Ismat means holding back: as a term, a letter being heavier and slower to say, in the other twenty-three letters. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَفِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ الحُرُوفِ المُذْلَقَهْ» (and «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ» are the fluent letters).
idea.kidsLead: Six letters are light and quick on the tongue; they come from the tip of the tongue or the lips. We gather them in «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ». The other letters are a little heavier.

how.text: Faa, raa, meem, noon, laam and baa: «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ».
Raa, noon and laam come from the tip of the tongue; faa, baa and meem from the lips.
Twenty-three letters: all the others.
They are called "held back" because they cannot build an Arabic word of four or five root letters alone: such a word nearly always has a fluent letter.
It is a feature of the language that helps with word roots; it brings no rule in recitation, as tafkhim or qalqalah do.

idea.note: Idhlaq and ismat leave no mark on how letters sound, as hams and jahr do, so many teachers pass over them quickly. They are the last of the five pairs of opposite sifat.

lessons.title: The characteristics without opposites
lessons.lede: Seven sifat have no opposites: safir (whistle), qalqalah, leen, inhiraf, takrir (rolling), tafashshi (spreading) and istitalah (lengthening).

idea.lead: There are seven sifat without opposites, each with a few letters of its own: safir in saad, zay and seen; qalqalah in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ»; leen in waw and yaa with sukun after a fathah; inhiraf in laam and raa; takrir in raa; tafashshi in sheen; and istitalah in daad. Ibn al-Jazari says: «صَفِيرُهَا صَادٌ وَزَايٌ سِينُ، قَلْقَلَةٌ قُطْبُ جَدٍّ وَاللِّينُ، وَاوٌ وَيَاءٌ سَكَنَا وَانْفَتَحَا، قَبْلَهُمَا وَالِانْحِرَافُ صُحِّحَا، فِي اللَّامِ وَالرَّا وَبِتَكْرِيرٍ جُعِلْ، وَلِلتَّفَشِّي الشِّينُ ضَادًا اسْتَطِلْ» (its whistling letters are saad, zay and seen; qalqalah is «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ»; leen is waw and yaa with sukun after a fathah; inhiraf is in laam and raa, and raa has takrir; sheen spreads, and daad lengthens).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters have special features: «ص ز س» have a sound like a bird's whistle; the air of «ش» spreads in the mouth; the sound of «ض» runs along the side of the tongue; and with «ر» the tip of the tongue trembles a little.

how.text: An extra sound like a bird's whistle, in saad, zay and seen: «ٱلصَّمَدُ», «ٱلۡوَسۡوَاسِ».
The makhraj bouncing in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ» with sukun; lesson 14 covers it.
Waw and yaa with sukun after a fathah, said with ease: «خَوۡفٍ», «بَيۡتٍ». Lesson 31.
A letter turning, after it comes out, away from its makhraj: laam towards the tip of the tongue, raa a little towards its back.
The tip of the tongue trembling with raa. It is learned so as to avoid it: say raa with one light tremble, especially with a shaddah: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».
The air spreading through the mouth with sheen: «شَرِّ».
The sound of daad running from the front to the back of the side of the tongue: «وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ».

idea.note: Some scholars list more, such as ghunnah in noon and meem, and khafa' (faintness) in the madd letters and haa. The most common mistakes here are rolling the raa too much, and losing the istitalah of daad until it sounds like a heavy dal.

lessons.title: Heavy and light letters (tafkhim and tarqiq)
lessons.lede: Tafkhim makes a letter heavy, so the mouth fills with its sound; tarqiq makes it light. The raised letters are always heavy; the low letters are light, except raa and laam in some cases; alif follows the letter before it.

idea.lead: In Arabic, tafkhim means fattening. As a term, it is a fullness in the sound of a letter, so that the mouth fills with its echo. Tarqiq means thinning: a lightness in the sound, so that the mouth does not fill. Letters are of three kinds. The seven raised letters are always heavy. The low letters are always light, except three: raa and the laam in the name Allah, which have their own lessons, and alif, which follows the letter before it. Ibn al-Jazari says: «فَرَقِّقَنْ مُسْتَفِلًا مِنْ أَحْرُفِ، وَحَاذِرَنْ تَفْخِيمَ لَفْظِ الأَلِفِ» (make the low letters light, and beware of making alif heavy).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters we read full, as if the mouth is filled with sound, like «ص», «ق» and «ط». Others are light and thin, like «س», «ك» and «ت». Alif takes on the letter before it: full in «قَالَ», light in «كَانَ».

how.text: The raised letters have five degrees: with fathah and an alif after «قَالَ», then with fathah «قَتَلَ», then dammah «قُتِلَ», then sukun «يَقۡتُلُ», then kasrah «قِيلَ».
It follows the letter before it: heavy in «قَالَ» and «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», light in «كَانَ» and «مَالِكِ».
They stay light even next to a heavy letter: the baa in «بَٰطِلٞ», the taa in «تَطۡهِيرٗا», the seen in «يَسۡطُونَ».
The ghunnah of a hidden noon or meem follows the letter after it: heavy before a raised letter «مِن قَبۡلُ», light before a low one.
They have their own rules: lesson 39 for raa, lesson 40 for the laam in the name Allah.

idea.note: Some scholars count three degrees of tafkhim; others five, as above. Mistakes: making a low letter heavy next to a heavy one, making alif heavy after a light letter, or making a raised letter light with a kasrah.

quiz.why: Baa is a low letter: it stays light even next to a heavy letter.

options: Heavy, since a raised letter comes after it
quiz.why: The ghunnah of ikhfa' follows the letter after it; qaaf is raised, so it is heavy.

quiz.q: Which low letters are heavy in some cases?
options: Raa, the laam in Allah, and alif
quiz.why: Raa and the laam in the name Allah have their own rules, and alif follows the letter before it.

lessons.title: The rules of raa
lessons.lede: Raa is heavy with a fathah or dammah, or with sukun after a fathah or dammah. It is light with a kasrah, or with sukun after an original kasrah and no raised letter after it.

formula.caption: With sukun: depends on the letter before

idea.lead: Raa is a low letter, but it is heavy or light depending on its vowel and what comes before it. It is heavy with a fathah or dammah «رَبِّ», «رُزِقُواْ»; with sukun after a fathah or dammah «مَرۡيَمَ», «ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ»; with sukun after a temporary kasrah «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ»; or after an original kasrah with a raised letter, without kasrah, after it in its word «مِرۡصَادٗا». It is light with a kasrah «رِجَالٞ», or with sukun after an original kasrah with no raised letter after it in its word «فِرۡعَوۡنَ».
idea.kidsLead: We read raa full when it has a fathah or a dammah «رَبِّ», «رُزِقُوا», and light when it has a kasrah «رِجَالٌ». When it has a sukun, we look at the letter before it: full after fathah and dammah, usually light after kasrah «فِرْعَوْنَ».

how.text: With fathah «رَبِّ», dammah «رُزِقُواْ», or sukun after fathah «مَرۡيَمَ» or dammah «ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ».
With sukun after a temporary kasrah «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ», or after an original kasrah with a raised letter, without kasrah, after it in its word: «قِرۡطَاسٖ», «مِرۡصَادٗا», «فِرۡقَةٖ».
With kasrah «رِجَالٞ», or with sukun after an original kasrah and no raised letter after it: «فِرۡعَوۡنَ», «وَٱغۡفِرۡ لَنَا».

A raa you stop on is light after a yaa with sukun «خَيۡرٞ», «قَدِيرٞ», or after a kasrah «مُّنتَشِرٞ», or after a low letter with sukun that follows a kasrah «ٱلذِّكۡرِ»; otherwise it is heavy «ٱلۡقَدۡرِ».

In «فِرۡقٖ» (Ash-Shu'ara 63), heavy or light. When stopping on «مِصۡرَ» and «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ», both are allowed; Ibn al-Jazari chose heavy for «مِصۡرَ» and light for «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ». Stopping on «يَسۡرِ», «أَنۡ أَسۡرِ», «فَأَسۡرِ» and «وَنُذُرِ» also has two ways.

idea.note: Hafs has one imalah in the whole Quran, in «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا» (Hud 41): the raa and the alif after it lean towards kasrah and yaa, and the raa is light. Mistakes: rolling the raa, or making a light raa heavy after a kasrah.

lessons.title: The laam in the name Allah
lessons.lede: The laam in the name Allah is heavy after a fathah or dammah, and light after a kasrah.

idea.lead: Laam is a low letter and always light, except the laam in the name Allah, «ٱللَّه» and «ٱللَّهُمَّ». It is heavy after a fathah or dammah, as in «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», «رُسُلُ ٱللَّهِ» and «هُوَ ٱللَّهُ», or when you start with it, since the joining hamzah then has a fathah. It is light after a kasrah, original or temporary, as in «بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ», «لِلَّهِ» and «قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ».
idea.kidsLead: In the name «ٱللَّه», we read the laam full when a fathah or dammah comes before it «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», and light when a kasrah comes before it «بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ».

how.text: «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», «شَهِدَ ٱللَّهُ»: heavy.
«رُسُلُ ٱللَّهِ», «هُوَ ٱللَّهُ»: heavy.
«ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ»: heavy, since the joining hamzah before it has a fathah.
«بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ», «لِلَّهِ», «بِٱللَّهِ»: light.
Light after a temporary kasrah too: «قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ»; and after tanween given a kasrah to join: «أَحَدٌ ۝ ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ», when read together.

idea.note: This rule is only for the laam in the name Allah; every other laam is light, even next to a heavy letter: «وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ», «وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ». A common mistake is making the laam heavy in «لِلَّهِ» and «بِٱللَّهِ».

lessons.title: Daad and dhaa (ض and ظ)
lessons.lede: Daad and dhaa share most of their sifat, but differ in makhraj and in istitalah. Mixing them up is clear lahn and changes the meaning.

formula.caption: Side of the tongue with the molars
Tongue tip with the front teeth

idea.lead: Daad and dhaa are both voiced, rikhw, raised, covered and musmat; they differ in two things: makhraj and istitalah. Daad comes from one or both sides of the tongue against the upper molars, and its sound runs along the side: this is istitalah. Dhaa comes from the tip of the tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth. Mixing them up is clear lahn: «نَّاضِرَةٌ» means radiant, and «نَاظِرَةٞ» means looking. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالضَّادَ بِاسْتِطَالَةٍ وَمَخْرَجِ، مَيِّزْ مِنَ الظَّاءِ وَكُلُّهَا تَجِي» (tell daad from dhaa by istitalah and makhraj).
idea.kidsLead: «ض» and «ظ» are two full letters that sound alike. «ض» comes from the side of the tongue with the back teeth, and its sound runs on. For «ظ», the tip of the tongue comes out a little between the front teeth. Careful: «نَاضِرَةٌ» means bright and beautiful, and «نَاظِرَةٌ» means looking.

how.text: From the side of the tongue against the upper molars (the left side is easier and more common), with the sound running along the side.
From the tip of the tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth; the tip comes out a little.
Jahr, rakhawah, isti'la', itbaq and ismat.
«نَّاضِرَةٌ» and «نَاظِرَةٞ» (Al-Qiyamah 22 and 23); «ضَلَّ» (went astray) and «ظَلَّ» (became).
Saying daad as a heavy dal, or as dhaa; or saying dhaa as a heavy zay.

idea.note: Hafs reads «وَمَا هُوَ عَلَى ٱلۡغَيۡبِ بِضَنِينٖ» (At-Takwir 24) with daad, meaning "stingy"; others read it with dhaa, meaning "suspected". Daad is one of the hardest letters to say: learn it from a teacher, by listening and repeating.

lessons.title: Identical, related and close letters
lessons.lede: When two letters meet, they are identical if they share makhraj and sifat, related if they share makhraj but not sifat, and close if their makharij or sifat are near. When the first has a sukun, it usually merges into the second.

idea.lead: Two letters that meet are of three kinds. Identical (mutamathilan): the same makhraj and sifat, such as baa and baa. Related (mutajanisan): the same makhraj, different sifat, such as taa and dal, taa and taa (ط), thaa and dhaal, dhaal and dhaa (ظ), or baa and meem. Close (mutaqariban): near in makhraj or sifat, such as laam and raa, or qaaf and kaaf. Each kind has three cases: minor, when the first has a sukun and the second a vowel; major, when both have vowels; and absolute, when the first has a vowel and the second a sukun. It is mainly the minor case that merges.
idea.kidsLead: When a letter with sukun is followed by the same letter or one close to it, we merge the first into the second and read them as one doubled letter: «قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ» is read «قَتَّبَيَّنَ», and «قُلْ رَبِّ» is read «قُرَّبِّ».

how.text: The minor case always merges: «رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمۡ», «ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ»; except when the first is a madd letter: «قَالُواْ وَهُمۡ», «فِي يَوۡمٍ».
Hafs merges the minor case in: «قَد تَّبَيَّنَ», «أَثۡقَلَت دَّعَوَا», «وَدَّت طَّآئِفَةٞ», «إِذ ظَّلَمُوٓاْ», «يَلۡهَث ذَّٰلِكَ», «ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا».
Taa (ط) into taa (ت) is a partial idgham, keeping the covering (itbaq): «بَسَطتَ», «أَحَطتُ», «فَرَّطتُ».
The minor case merges with laam and raa «قُل رَّبِّ», and qaaf and kaaf «أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم» (Al-Mursalat 20), fully or partially, full being better known.
Hafs keeps them apart, except in a few words, such as «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» (Yusuf 11, lesson 47) and «مَكَّنِّي» (Al-Kahf 95).

idea.note: Hafs pauses (saktah) on «بَلۡۜ» in «بَلۡۜ رَانَ» (Al-Mutaffifin 14), so the laam does not merge into the raa. In «مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ» (Al-Haqqah 28 and 29) he has two ways: a pause with the letters clear, or merging. The idgham of noon sakinah into «يَرْمَلُونَ» (lessons 18 and 19) and the sun laam (lesson 15) belong here too.

lessons.title: The connecting and the cutting hamzah
lessons.lede: The cutting hamzah is said both when starting and when joining; the connecting hamzah is said when starting and dropped when joining.

idea.lead: The cutting hamzah (hamzat al-qat') is said both when starting and when joining. It comes in nouns, verbs and particles, as in «أَنۡعَمۡتَ» and «إِنَّ». The connecting hamzah (hamzat al-wasl) is an extra hamzah that lets you start on a letter with sukun: it is said when starting and dropped when joining, as in «ٱهۡدِنَا» and «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ». In the Mushaf it is an alif with a small head of saad «ٱ». Its vowel when starting: fathah in «ال»; kasrah in nouns; and in verbs, dammah if the third letter has a fixed dammah, kasrah if it has a fathah or kasrah.
idea.kidsLead: Some hamzahs we always read, like «أَنْعَمْتَ». Others we read only when we start with the word, and drop when we join it to the word before, like «ٱهْدِنَا»: we start «اِهْدِنَا», and join «وَٱهْدِنَا» as «وَهْدِنَا».

how.text: Said when starting and joining; written on an alif, under it, or alone: «أَنۡعَمۡتَ», «إِنَّ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ».

The hamzah of «ال», seven nouns in the Quran «ٱبۡن», «ٱبۡنَت», «ٱمۡرُؤٌ», «ٱمۡرَأَت», «ٱثۡنَانِ», «ٱثۡنَتَانِ», «ٱسۡم», and the verbal nouns of five- and six-letter verbs: «ٱنتِقَامٖ», «ٱسۡتِغۡفَارُ».
The past and command of five- and six-letter verbs, and the command of three-letter verbs: «ٱنطَلَقُواْ», «ٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡ», «ٱقۡرَأۡ».
Fathah in «ال»; kasrah in nouns; in verbs, dammah if the third letter has a fixed dammah «ٱدۡعُ» read «اُدۡعُ», kasrah if it has a fathah or kasrah «ٱذۡهَبۡ», «ٱضۡرِب».
Kasrah in «ٱمۡشُواْ», «ٱقۡضُوٓاْ», «ٱبۡنُواْ» and «ٱئۡتُواْ», since the dammah on their third letter is temporary; it was a kasrah.

idea.note: When starting with «ٱلِٱسۡمُ» in «بِئۡسَ ٱلِٱسۡمُ» (Al-Hujurat 11), Hafs has two ways: «أَلِسۡمُ», with the joining hamzah, or «لِسۡمُ», without it. When the question hamzah comes before a joining hamzah, the joining hamzah drops, as in «أَسۡتَغۡفَرۡتَ» (Al-Munafiqun 6); except with «ال», where it becomes an alif or is eased, as in lesson 30.
