lessons.title: Stopping and starting (waqf and ibtida')
lessons.lede: Waqf is stopping the sound on a word long enough to breathe, meaning to go on reading. Its main kind, the chosen stop, is complete, sufficient, good or bad.

formula.caption: starting where the meaning stands alone

idea.lead: Waqf is stopping the sound on a word long enough to breathe, meaning to go on reading. Saktah is stopping it briefly without a breath; qat' is ending the recitation. Some early scholars called knowing where to stop and start half of tajweed, since the meaning depends on it. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَبَعْدَ تَجْوِيدِكَ لِلْحُرُوفِ، لَا بُدَّ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ الوُقُوفِ، وَالِابْتِدَاءِ وَهْيَ تُقْسَمُ إِذَنْ، ثَلَاثَةً تَامٌّ وَكَافٍ وَحَسَنْ» (after perfecting the letters, you must know the stops and starts; they are of three kinds: complete, sufficient and good). By reason, stops are of four kinds: forced, waiting, testing and chosen; the chosen stop is complete, sufficient, good or bad.
idea.kidsLead: We stop in our reading to breathe, but we choose a place where the meaning is complete, like the end of an ayah. We do not stop in the middle of a phrase so the meaning changes, and we start again from a word where the meaning is right.

how.text: Because of running out of breath, a sneeze or forgetting: stop where you must, then start where the meaning is sound.
Waiting: stopping on a word with several readings to give them all, when combining riwayahs. Testing: in teaching, when asked about a stop.
On a phrase whose meaning is finished, with no link to what follows in wording or meaning: «وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 5).
Linked to what follows in meaning but not in wording: «أَمۡ لَمۡ تُنذِرۡهُمۡ لَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 6).
Linked to what follows in wording and meaning: fine to stop on, but not to start after: «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ».
No meaning is complete, or it suggests a wrong meaning: stopping on «بِسۡمِ», or on «إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَسۡتَحۡيِۦٓ» (Al-Baqarah 26).

idea.note: Most scholars hold that stopping at the end of each ayah is sunnah, even when what follows is linked to it, as with «رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ». After a good stop that is not at an ayah's end, start again from a little before, so the meaning joins. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَلَيْسَ فِي القُرْآنِ مِنْ وَقْفٍ وَجَبْ، وَلَا حَرَامٌ غَيْرُ مَا لَهُ سَبَبْ» (no stop in the Quran is required or forbidden, except for a reason).

quiz.q: What is waqf?
options: Stopping the sound long enough to breathe, meaning to go on
quiz.why: Waqf is stopping the sound on a word long enough to breathe, meaning to go on reading.

quiz.q: How does waqf differ from saktah?
options: Saktah is a shorter stop without a breath
quiz.why: Saktah stops the sound briefly without a breath; waqf comes with a breath.

quiz.q: What is a complete stop?
options: One linked to what follows in wording
One where no meaning is complete
On a finished phrase, with no link to what follows in wording or meaning
quiz.why: A complete stop is on a finished phrase cut off from what follows, as at the end of a story.

quiz.q: Stopping on «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ» is:
quiz.why: It gives a sound meaning, but «رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» after it is linked in wording: a good stop.

quiz.q: Stopping on «إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَسۡتَحۡيِۦٓ» is:
quiz.why: It suggests a wrong meaning, so it is bad: join it to what follows.

quiz.q: What is the ruling on stopping at the end of each ayah?
quiz.why: Stopping at the end of each ayah is sunnah, even when what follows is linked to it.

quiz.q: What is a forced stop?
options: A stop for lack of breath or a sneeze
A stop to give all the readings
A stop at the end of an ayah
quiz.why: You stop where you must, then start where the meaning is sound.

lessons.title: Stop signs in the Mushaf
lessons.lede: The Madinah Mushaf has six signs over the words, showing the reader where to stop and where to join.

idea.lead: Scholars put signs over the words in the Mushaf to guide the reader on stopping and joining, from their understanding of the meaning. The Madinah Mushaf has six: «مـ» for a required stop; «لا» for "do not stop"; «ج» for an allowed stop, stopping and joining being equal; «صلى» for an allowed stop where joining is better; «قلى» for an allowed stop where stopping is better; and «∴ ∴» for linked stops (ta'anuq).
idea.kidsLead: In the Mushaf, small signs over the words tell us where to stop: «مـ» means stop here, «لا» means do not stop, and «ج», «صلى» and «قلى» mean you may stop. The three dots come twice: stop at only one of them.

how.text: Required stop: stop here, since joining suggests a wrong meaning: «إِنَّمَا يَسۡتَجِيبُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡمَعُونَۘ وَٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰ يَبۡعَثُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ».
Do not stop here; if you do, go back a little and read on. At the end of an ayah, stopping is allowed.
Stopping is allowed, stopping and joining being equal: «وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡهُۚ».
Stopping is allowed, but joining is better: «فَزَادَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مَرَضٗاۖ».
Stopping is allowed, and stopping is better: «إِلَّا قَلِيلٞۗ».
Linked stops: if you stop at one of the two places, do not stop at the other: «لَا رَيۡبَۛ فِيهِۛ».

idea.note: These are the signs of the Madinah Mushaf; other Mushafs may differ. They come from scholars' understanding of the meaning: the required stop is kept, and the others are guidance. Stopping at the end of each ayah is sunnah.

ayat.findHint: Find the stop sign over the words in each ayah and what it means, then bring the colours back to check.

why: «مـ» over «يَسۡمَعُونَ»: a required stop, so the dead are not taken to answer with those who hear
«صلى» over «مَرَضٗا»: stopping is allowed, joining is better
«ج» over «وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡهُ»: stopping and joining are equal
The linked-stop dots over «رَيۡبَ» and «فِيهِ»: stop on only one

ayat.tip: The sign is written small over the last letter of the word, as you can see in the ayahs above.

quiz.q: What does «مـ» over a word mean?
quiz.why: «مـ» marks a required stop, since joining suggests a wrong meaning.

quiz.q: What does «لا» over a word mean?
quiz.why: «لا» means do not stop; if you do, go back a little, except at the end of an ayah.

quiz.q: What does «صلى» mean?
quiz.why: «صلى» means you may stop, but joining is better.

quiz.q: What does «قلى» mean?
quiz.why: «قلى» means you may stop, and stopping is better.

quiz.q: What does «ج» mean?
options: Stopping allowed, stopping and joining equal
quiz.why: «ج» means stopping and joining are equal.

quiz.q: How do you read «لَا رَيۡبَۛ فِيهِۛ هُدٗى», with the linked-stop dots?
options: Stop at only one of them
quiz.why: With linked stops, if you stop at one place, you do not stop at the other.

quiz.q: Why is stopping required in «يَسۡمَعُونَۘ وَٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰ»?
options: Joining suggests the dead answer with those who hear
quiz.why: Allah raises the dead; they do not answer with those who hear. Joining would suggest a wrong meaning.

lessons.title: The brief pauses (saktat)
lessons.lede: Saktah is stopping the sound briefly, without a breath, meaning to go on reading. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, has four required pauses when joining.

formula.caption: a brief stop of the sound

idea.lead: Saktah is stopping the sound briefly, for about two counts, without a breath, meaning to go on reading. It happens only where it has come down from the reciters, and the Mushaf marks it with a small seen «ۜ» over the letter. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, has four required pauses when joining: on «عِوَجَاۜ» in Al-Kahf, «مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜ» in Ya-Sin, «مَنۡۜ» in Al-Qiyamah, and «بَلۡۜ» in Al-Mutaffifin.
idea.kidsLead: A saktah is a very short stop, without taking a breath; then we go on reading. Hafs has four places where we pause, such as «مَنْ ۜ رَاقٍ» and «بَلْ ۜ رَانَ». The sign is a small seen over the letter.

how.text: «وَلَمۡ يَجۡعَل لَّهُۥ عِوَجَاۜ ۝ قَيِّمٗا» (Al-Kahf 1 and 2), when the two ayahs are joined.
«مَنۢ بَعَثَنَا مِن مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜۗ هَٰذَا» (Ya-Sin 52).
«وَقِيلَ مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ» (Al-Qiyamah 27): the noon is said clearly and does not merge into the raa.
«كَلَّاۖ بَلۡۜ رَانَ» (Al-Mutaffifin 14): the laam is said clearly and does not merge into the raa.
«مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ» (Al-Haqqah 28 and 29): a pause with the letters clear, or merging. Between Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah: stop, pause or join (lesson 4).

idea.note: The pauses keep away a wrong meaning: in «عِوَجَا قَيِّمًا», so that «قَيِّمًا» (upright) is not taken to describe «عِوَجَا» (crookedness); in «مَرۡقَدِنَا هَٰذَا», so that «هَٰذَا» is not taken to describe the resting place. When you stop on the word itself, there is no saktah: the stop does its work.

ayat.findHint: Find the pause sign in each ayah, and listen to how the reciter stops the sound without a breath, then bring the colours back to check.

why: A pause on the noon, so it does not merge into the raa
A pause on the laam, so it does not merge into the raa
A pause on the alif of «مَّرۡقَدِنَا», then «هَٰذَا»

ayat.tip: The Mushaf marks the pause with a small seen «ۜ» over the letter, as you can see in the ayahs above.

quiz.q: What is saktah?
options: Stopping the sound briefly without a breath
quiz.why: Saktah is stopping the sound briefly, without a breath, meaning to go on reading.

quiz.q: How many required pauses does Hafs have by way of ash-Shatibiyyah?
quiz.why: Four: on «عِوَجَاۜ», «مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜ», «مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ» and «بَلۡۜ رَانَ».

quiz.q: Where is the pause in Surah Al-Kahf?
quiz.why: You pause on «عِوَجَاۜ» when joining it to «قَيِّمٗا».

quiz.q: How does the Mushaf mark a pause?
quiz.why: The pause sign is a small seen over the letter.

quiz.q: Why the pause in «مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ»?
options: So the noon does not merge into the raa and sound like one word
quiz.why: With the pause the noon is said clearly, so it does not become «مَرَّاق», as if one word.

quiz.q: What are the two ways for Hafs in «مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ»?
options: A pause with the letters clear, or merging
quiz.why: You may pause on the haa and say it clearly, or merge it into the haa after it.

quiz.q: Do you pause on «عِوَجَا» when you stop on it?
options: No: the stop does the work of the pause
The pause is better than the stop
quiz.why: Saktah is for joining; when you stop on the word, there is no saktah.

lessons.title: Stopping with sukun, rawm and ishmam
lessons.lede: You stop on the end of a word with a plain sukun; rawm is allowed with dammah and kasrah, and ishmam with dammah only.

formula.caption: part of the vowel: dammah, kasrah

idea.lead: The basic way to stop is a plain sukun, dropping the vowel completely. Rawm is saying part of the vowel in a faint voice that only someone near can hear; it is for dammah and kasrah, not fathah. Ishmam is rounding the lips after giving the last letter a sukun, silently, as a sign of the dammah: the seeing can see it and the blind cannot hear it; it is for dammah only. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَحَاذِرِ الوَقْفَ بِكُلِّ الحَرَكَهْ، إِلَّا إِذَا رُمْتَ فَبَعْضُ الحَرَكَهْ، إِلَّا بِفَتْحٍ أَوْ بِنَصْبٍ وَأَشِمّْ، إِشَارَةً بِالضَّمِّ فِي رَفْعٍ وَضَمّْ» (beware of stopping with the whole vowel, except with rawm, which is part of it, but not with fathah; and use ishmam to point to the dammah).
idea.kidsLead: When we stop on the end of a word, we read it with sukun: «نَسْتَعِينْ». We may let a tiny bit of the dammah or kasrah be heard: this is rawm. Or we round our lips after the sukun, silently: this is ishmam, only with dammah.

how.text: Allowed on any word ending in a vowel: «نَسۡتَعِينۡ», «ٱلرَّحِيمۡ».
With dammah and kasrah: say the dammah of «نَسۡتَعِينُ» or the kasrah of «ٱلرَّحِيمِ» faintly, about a third of the vowel.
With dammah only: give the noon of «نَسۡتَعِينُ» a sukun, then round the lips silently.
Fathah; the feminine haa «رَحۡمَةۡ»; the plural meem «عَلَيۡهِمۡ»; or a temporary vowel, as when stopping on «قُمۡ» from «قُمِ ٱلَّيۡلَ».
With rawm, the madd for stopping is only two counts; with sukun and ishmam, two, four or six.

idea.note: In «لَا تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» (Yusuf 11), Hafs has two ways when joining: ishmam, merging the two noons, or rawm, keeping them apart. The word was «تَأۡمَنُنَا», with two noons. Learn rawm and ishmam from a teacher, by listening and repeating.

ayat.legendNoon: The place of ishmam or rawm
ayat.findHint: Listen to «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» and look at the mark under the meem, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Ishmam at the doubled noon, or rawm with both noons clear

ayat.tip: The small diamond under the meem of «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» in the Mushaf marks ishmam or rawm, in this word alone.

quiz.q: What is rawm?
options: Saying part of the vowel in a faint voice
quiz.why: Rawm is saying part of the vowel in a faint voice that only someone near can hear.

quiz.q: What is ishmam?
options: Rounding the lips after the sukun, silently
quiz.why: Ishmam is rounding the lips after the sukun, silently, as a sign of the dammah.

quiz.q: With which vowel is ishmam used?
quiz.why: Ishmam points to the dammah, so it is only for a dammah.

quiz.q: With which vowel is rawm not allowed?
quiz.why: Rawm is for dammah and kasrah, not fathah.

quiz.q: Is rawm allowed when stopping on «رَحۡمَةٞ»?
options: No: it is a feminine haa, stopped on with a haa
quiz.why: The feminine haa is stopped on with sukun, so it takes neither rawm nor ishmam.

quiz.q: With rawm on «نَسۡتَعِينُ», how long is the madd?
quiz.why: With rawm the sukun is not complete, so only two counts are allowed.

quiz.q: What are the two ways for Hafs in «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا»?
options: Ishmam with idgham, or rawm with izhar
quiz.why: Ishmam with the two noons merged, or rawm with both noons clear.

lessons.title: Common mistakes in pronouncing the letters
lessons.lede: Common mistakes in saying the letters that scholars warn about, and some words Hafs reads in his own way.

idea.lead: After the makharij, the sifat and the rules, scholars point out mistakes that often happen in saying the letters, so the reader can avoid them. Ibn al-Jazari says: «فَرَقِّقَنْ مُسْتَفِلًا مِنْ أَحْرُفِ، وَحَاذِرَنْ تَفْخِيمَ لَفْظِ الأَلِفِ، وَهَمْزَ الحَمْدُ أَعُوذُ اهْدِنَا، اللهِ ثُمَّ لَامَ لِلَّهِ لَنَا» (make the low letters light, beware of making alif heavy, and the hamzah of «الحمد», «أعوذ», «اهدنا» and «الله», and the laam of «لله» and «لنا»). The most common mistakes are swapping letters that sound alike, making light letters heavy, losing the ghunnah, and getting the madd lengths wrong.
idea.kidsLead: In this lesson we gather small mistakes many readers make, so we watch out for them: we do not turn 'ayn into a hamzah or haa (ح) into haa (ه); we do not make light letters heavy; and we keep the ghunnah and give each madd its length.

how.text: Said fully and light, not eased and not over-pressed, especially at the start of «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ», «أَعُوذُ» and «ٱهۡدِنَا» when starting.
Make it clear when it repeats or follows an alif: «جِبَاهُهُمۡ», «وُجُوهَهُمۡ», «فِيهِ هُدٗى».
Do not turn 'ayn into a hamzah or haa (ح) into haa (ه): «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ», «ٱلرَّحِيمِ».
Light, not heavy before a heavy letter, and with qalqalah when it has sukun: «بَٰطِلٞ», «بِٱلۡحَقِّ».
Keep the covering of taa (ط) in «بَسَطتَ» and «أَحَطتُ», and the whisper of taa (ت), without qalqalah: «فَتَنَّا».
Make their doubled ghunnah clear, but no longer than two counts: «ثُمَّ», «إِنَّ».
Do not roll the raa; make laam heavy only in the name Allah: «وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ», «وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ».

idea.note: Hafs has his own readings in some words: «يَبۡصُطُ» (Al-Baqarah 245) and «بَصۡطَةٗ» (Al-A'raf 69) are written with saad and read with seen, with a small seen over the saad. «ٱلۡمُصَيۡطِرُونَ» (At-Tur 37) is read with seen or saad, and «بِمُصَيۡطِرٍ» (Al-Ghashiyah 22) with saad. In «ضَعۡفٖ» and «ضَعۡفٗا» (Ar-Rum 54), the daad may take fathah or dammah, fathah being preferred. He eases the second hamzah in «أَأَعۡجَمِيّٞ» (Fussilat 44).

quiz.q: How is the hamzah of «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» said when starting?
quiz.why: The hamzah is said fully and light, without easing or extra pressure.

quiz.q: How is the baa in «بَٰطِلٞ» said?
quiz.why: Baa is a low letter: it is light, even next to the heavy taa (ط).

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «يَبۡصُطُ» in Al-Baqarah?
quiz.why: It is written with saad, and Hafs reads it with seen; a small seen is written over the saad.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «بِمُصَيۡطِرٍ» in Al-Ghashiyah?
quiz.why: Hafs reads it with saad; «ٱلۡمُصَيۡطِرُونَ» in At-Tur has both ways.

quiz.q: What does Hafs prefer in «ضَعۡفٖ» in Surah Ar-Rum?
quiz.why: Hafs has fathah and dammah on the daad; fathah is preferred.

quiz.q: What is the mistake to avoid with the haa in «جِبَاهُهُمۡ»?
options: Hiding it, or merging the two haas
quiz.why: When haa repeats, it is made clear: neither hidden nor merged.

quiz.q: What is the mistake to avoid in «بَسَطتَ»?
options: Merging the taa (ط) fully, losing its covering
Saying the seen from its makhraj
quiz.why: The idgham here is partial: the covering of taa (ط) stays.
